questions.stem: What is $$\int_{-1}^{2} \left(-3x^{2} - 4x + 3\right)dx$$?

options.why: This subtracts values of the integrand instead of an antiderivative.
Correct. An antiderivative is $$F(x) = -x^{3} - 2x^{2} + 3x$$; $$F(2) - F(-1) = -6$$.
This adds F(a) instead of subtracting it.
This is F(b) only; subtract F(a) as well.

questions.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $$\int_{-1}^{2} f(x)\,dx = F(2) - F(-1)$$ with $$F(x) = -x^{3} - 2x^{2} + 3x$$. That is $$-10 - (-4) = -6$$.

questions.stem: At what value of $$x$$ does the graph of $$f(x) = x^{3} - 9x^{2} + 6x + 1$$ have a point of inflection?

options.why: Correct. $$f''(x) = 6x - 18$$ is zero and changes sign at $$x = 3$$.

This is −b/(2a), the vertex formula for a parabola, applied to the cubic's coefficients. Set f″(x) = 0 instead.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = 3x^{2} - 18x + 6$$ and $$f''(x) = 6x - 18$$. $$f''$$ is linear, so it changes sign at its zero, $$x = 3$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6} + h\right) - \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)}{h}$$?

options.why: Sign error: $$\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$$ and $$\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x$$.
Correct. The limit is the derivative of $$\sin x$$ at $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$.
This is the function value at the point, not the derivative.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form.

questions.explanation: The expression is the definition of $$f'\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$$ for $$f(x) = \sin x$$, which equals $$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$.

options.why: Correct. Multiply each subinterval's width by the appropriate height and add.

questions.stem: A quantity $$y$$ satisfies $$\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$$ and doubles every 4 hours. What is the value of $$k$$?

options.why: This is not a solution of e^{kT} = 2.
Doubling means e^{kT} = 2; solve with a logarithm.
Correct. $$y = y_0e^{kt}$$ and $$e^{4k} = 2$$.
Solving $$4k = \ln 2$$ requires dividing by $$4$$.

questions.stem: A twice-differentiable function $$f$$ satisfies $$f'(2) = 0$$ and $$f''(2) = 6$$. Which of the following must be true?

options.why: Correct. f′ = 0 and f″ > 0: the graph is concave up at a horizontal tangent.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} 4x - 6 & x < 1 \\ -x - 5 & x \geq 1 \end{cases}$$. What is $$\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)$$?

options.why: This is $$f(1)$$ and the right-hand limit only. The left-hand limit is $$-2$$.
A limit is never the average of the one-sided limits. When they differ, the limit does not exist.
Correct. The left-hand limit is $$-2$$ and the right-hand limit is $$-6$$. They differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
This is the left-hand limit only. The right-hand limit is $$-6$$.

questions.explanation: From the left, $$f(x) = 4x - 6 \to -2$$. From the right, $$f(x) = -x - 5 \to -6$$. Since $$-2 \neq -6$$, $$\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)$$ does not exist.

questions.stem: Using the line tangent to $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ at $$x = 81$$, what is the approximation of $$\sqrt{80}$$?

options.why: Sign error: the change in x is added, not subtracted.
The derivative of $$\sqrt{x}$$ is $$\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$$; this forgets the 2.
This uses slope $$\frac{1}{2}$$ instead of $$f'(81) = \frac{1}{18}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sin(x^{5})\right)$$?

options.why: This leaves out the derivative of the inside function.
This makes a sign or coefficient error in the outer derivative.
Correct. This is the chain rule: the derivative of the outer function, evaluated at the inside, times the derivative of the inside.
This differentiates the inside but then substitutes it incorrectly into the outer derivative.

questions.explanation: Treat $$\sin(x^{5})$$ as a composite and apply the chain rule: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sin(x^{5})\right) = 5x^{4}\cos(x^{5})$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{-5x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 1}$$?

options.why: This is the ratio of the constant terms, which only matters as x approaches 0.
Correct. The degrees match, so the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients, $$-5$$.
The outputs grow without bound only when the numerator has the higher degree.
The limit is 0 only when the denominator has the higher degree.

questions.explanation: Divide the numerator and denominator by $$x^2$$: the expression becomes $$\frac{-5 + 1/x^2}{1 + 1/x^2}$$, which approaches $$-5$$.

questions.stem: If $$f(x) = \sec x$$, what is $$f'\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$$?

options.why: This value doesn't come from the correct derivative formula.
Check the sign: the derivatives of the co-functions (cot, csc) are negative; tan and sec are not.
Correct. $$f'(x) = \sec x \tan x$$, evaluated at $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$.
This mixes up the derivative with a different trigonometric value at the point.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sec x\right) = \sec x \tan x$$. Substituting $$x = \frac{\pi}{4}$$ gives $$\sqrt{2}$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = x^{2} + 3x$$. What value of $$c$$ satisfies the conclusion of the Mean Value Theorem for $$f$$ on the interval $$[-3, -1]$$?

options.why: This is where f′(c) = 0, the vertex, not where f′(c) equals the average rate of change.
The MVT guarantees a point strictly inside the interval, and this endpoint doesn't satisfy the equation.
Correct. The average rate of change is $$\frac{f(-1) - f(-3)}{2} = -1$$, and $$f'(c) = 2c + 3 = -1$$ gives $$c = -2$$.
The MVT guarantees a point strictly inside the interval, and this endpoint doesn't satisfy the equation.

questions.stem: On the open interval $$0 < x < 6$$, at how many values of $$x$$ does $$f$$ have a relative maximum?

options.why: A relative maximum of f occurs only where f′ changes from positive to negative; touching or crossing upward does not count.
A relative maximum of f occurs only where f′ changes from positive to negative; touching or crossing upward does not count.
Correct. Count the places where f′ crosses the x-axis from above to below.
A relative maximum of f occurs only where f′ changes from positive to negative; touching or crossing upward does not count.

questions.stem: Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x^2 - y$$ passing through the point $$(-1, -3)$$. What is $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ at that point?

options.why: This is dy/dx, the first derivative.
Correct. $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2x - \frac{dy}{dx}$$, and $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 4$$ at the point.
Sign error: the derivative of −y is −dy/dx.
This differentiates x² but treats y as a constant; y depends on x.

questions.explanation: Differentiate implicitly: $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2x - \frac{dy}{dx} = 2x - (x^2 - y)$$. At $$(-1, -3)$$: $$-2 - 4 = -6$$.

questions.stem: What is the value of $$\int_{0}^{3} f(x)\,dx$$?

options.why: This is the total area, treating regions below the axis as positive.
Correct. Add the areas above the x-axis and subtract the areas below it.
Sign error: regions above the axis count positive.
This is f(b) − f(a), the change in f, not the integral of f.

questions.explanation: Split $$[0, 3]$$ into unit intervals and add the signed areas of the trapezoids and triangles: the result is $$-\frac{3}{2}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{1} x\left(x^2 + 1\right)^{3}dx$$?

options.why: This evaluates only at the upper limit.
This forgets the factor $$\frac{1}{2}$$ from $$du = 2x\,dx$$.
After substituting, the limits must change to u-values (from c to 1 + c), not stay 0 to 1.
Correct. With $$u = x^2 + 1$$, $$du = 2x\,dx$$, the integral is $$\frac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{2} u^{3}\,du$$.

questions.stem: The region bounded by $$y = x^2$$, the x-axis, and the line $$x = 3$$ is revolved about the x-axis. What is the volume of the resulting solid?

options.why: The disc method has a factor of $$\pi$$.
$$(x^2)^2 = x^4$$, whose antiderivative is $$\frac{x^5}{5}$$.
This integrates the radius instead of the radius squared.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x + 1} - 1}{x}$$?

options.why: Correct. Rationalizing gives $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 1} + 1}$$, which approaches $$\frac{1}{2}$$.
This forgets that the conjugate denominator is $$\sqrt{x + 1} + 1$$, which approaches $$2$$, not $$1$$.
The expression is undefined at 0, but rationalizing shows the outputs approach a single number.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line tangent to the curve $$x^2 + y^2 = 169$$ at the point $$(-12, 5)$$?

options.why: Correct. $$2x + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$$ gives $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y} = -\frac{-12}{5}$$.
This is y/x. The tangent line is perpendicular to the radius, whose slope is y/x, so the tangent slope is −x/y.

questions.explanation: Differentiate implicitly: $$2x + 2y\,y' = 0$$, so $$y' = -\frac{x}{y}$$. At $$(-12, 5)$$ this is $$\frac{12}{5}$$.

questions.stem: The derivative of a function $$f$$ is $$f'(x) = (x + 3)^2(x + 1)$$. On which intervals is $$f$$ increasing?

options.why: Here f′ < 0 because $$x + 1 < 0$$.
On $$-3 < x < -1$$ the factor $$x + 1$$ is negative.
Correct. The squared factor is never negative, so the sign of $$f'$$ matches $$x + 1$$.
The squared factor does not change sign at $$x = -3$$, so f′ < 0 for $$x < -3$$.

questions.explanation: $$(x + 3)^2 \geq 0$$ for all $$x$$, so $$f'(x) > 0$$ exactly when $$x > -1$$. Note $$f'$$ does not change sign at $$-3$$, so there is no extremum there.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of $$y = x^2$$ and $$y = 4x$$?

options.why: An area is never negative; this subtracts the curves in the wrong order.
This is the area under the parabola alone.
This is the area under the line alone.
Correct. $$\int_0^{4} (4x - x^2)\,dx$$: top curve minus bottom curve.

questions.explanation: The curves meet at $$0$$ and $$4$$. Area $$= \int_0^{4} (4u - u^2)\,du = \frac{4u^2}{2} - \frac{u^3}{3}\Big|_0^{4} = \frac{32}{3}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos(6x)}{x^2}$$?

options.why: $$\frac{0}{0}$$ is indeterminate; it does not mean the limit is 0.
This differentiates the numerator and denominator but then inverts the ratio, or applies the rule incorrectly.

questions.explanation: Direct substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$. Differentiate the numerator and denominator separately (L'Hospital's Rule): $$\frac{6\sin(6x)}{2x} \to \frac{36\cos(6x)}{2}$$, which gives $$18$$.

questions.stem: The edge length of a cube is increasing at a constant rate of 5 centimeters per second. At the instant when the edge length is 6 centimeters, what is the rate of change of the volume?

questions.explanation: $$\frac{dV}{dt} = 3s^2\frac{ds}{dt}$$. Substitute the dimension $$6$$ and its rate $$5$$ to get $$540$$ (cubic or square centimeters per second).

The IVT only guarantees zeros where the sign changes; other zeros are possible but not required.

questions.explanation: Because $$f$$ is continuous, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a solution of $$f(x) = 0$$ on every interval where the values change sign. Counting the sign changes in the table gives 3.

questions.stem: Let $$R$$ be the region enclosed by $$y = x$$ and $$y = x^2$$. Which of the following gives the volume of the solid generated when $$R$$ is revolved about the line $$y = -1$$?

options.why: This squares the difference of the radii instead of subtracting their squares.

This revolves about the x-axis.

questions.stem: The function $$g$$ is defined by $$g(x) = \frac{\sin(4x)}{e^{3x} - 1}$$ for $$x \neq 0$$. For what value of $$g(0)$$ is $$g$$ continuous at $$x = 0$$?

options.why: The two small quantities do not shrink at the same rate.
Correct. Evaluating $$g$$ at inputs very close to 0 (or using the limits of $$\frac{\sin u}{u}$$ and $$\frac{e^u - 1}{u}$$) gives $$\frac{4}{3}$$.
This inverts the ratio.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, which is indeterminate, not 0.

questions.explanation: For continuity, $$g(0)$$ must equal $$\lim_{x \to 0} g(x)$$. Near 0, $$\sin(4x) \approx 4x$$ and $$e^{3x} - 1 \approx 3x$$, so the limit is $$\frac{4}{3} \approx 1.333$$. A table of values near 0 confirms it.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of $$y = 2\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$$ and $$y = x^2 - 1$$?

options.why: This adds the absolute values of the curves instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: The temperature of a room, in degrees Fahrenheit, is modeled by $$H(t) = 73 + 17\sin\left(\frac{t}{8}\right)e^{-t/20}$$, where $$t$$ is measured in hours. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the temperature at $$t = 14$$, in degrees Fahrenheit per hour?

options.why: Correct. The calculator's numerical derivative of $$H$$ at $$t = 14$$ gives -0.603; the temperature is decreasing.

questions.explanation: The instantaneous rate of change is $$H'(14) \approx -0.603$$ degrees Fahrenheit per hour, from the calculator's numerical derivative.

questions.stem: What is the absolute maximum value of $$f(x) = xe^{-x/5} + \frac{\sin x}{4}$$ on the interval $$[0, 9]$$?

questions.stem: Which of the following is the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x}{y}$$ with $$y(0) = 6$$?

options.why: The initial value is positive, so the positive root is needed.
At $$x = 0$$ this gives $$\sqrt{6}$$, not $$6$$: the constant must be $$6^2$$.
This would have dy/dx = 1, which is not x/y.
Correct. $$y\,dy = x\,dx$$ gives $$y^2 = x^2 + C$$; $$C = 36$$, and the positive root matches $$y(0) = 6$$.

questions.explanation: Separate: $$\int y\,dy = \int x\,dx$$, so $$\frac{y^2}{2} = \frac{x^2}{2} + C$$. With $$y(0) = 6$$, $$y^2 = x^2 + 36$$ and $$y = \sqrt{x^2 + 36}$$.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $$v(t) = 4\cos\left(\frac{t^2}{5}\right) - 0.5$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 4$$. At what time does the particle first change direction?

questions.stem: Sand is added to a pile at a rate modeled by $$R(t) = 17 + 4\sin\left(\frac{t}{6}\right)\sqrt{t + 1}$$ cubic feet per hour, for $$0 \leq t \leq 8$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the pile contains 55 cubic feet of sand. How much sand is in the pile at $$t = 8$$?

This assumes the rate stays at R(T) for the whole time.
This adds the rate at one instant, not the accumulated amount.

questions.explanation: Amount = initial amount + accumulated change = $$55 + \int_0^{8} R(t)\,dt \approx 55 + 180.926 = 235.926$$ cubic feet.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with velocity $$v(t) = 2\sin(t)\,e^{-t/6} + 0.3$$. What is the total distance the particle travels over $$0 \leq t \leq 5$$?

questions.explanation: Total distance $$= \int_0^{5} |v(t)|\,dt \approx 4.820$$. The displacement $$\int_0^{5} v(t)\,dt \approx 3.341$$ is smaller because the particle moves backward part of the time.

questions.stem: The derivative of a function $$f$$ is $$f'(x) = \sin\left(\frac{x^2}{4}\right) - 0.75\cos x$$. How many relative extrema does $$f$$ have on the open interval $$0 < x < 4$$?

questions.stem: Consider the curve $$x^2 - xy + y^2 = 48$$, for which $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y - 2x}{2y - x}$$. At which points on the curve is the tangent line horizontal?

questions.stem: Let $$R$$ be the region bounded by $$y = \sqrt{x}\,e^{-x/4} + 0.2$$, the x-axis, $$x = 0$$, and $$x = 4$$. What is the volume of the solid generated when $$R$$ is revolved about the line $$y = -2$$?

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + x + e^{x/3}$$, and let $$g$$ be the inverse of $$f$$. What is the value of $$g'(10)$$?

options.why: This evaluates $$f'$$ at $$10$$ instead of at the input where $$f(x) = 10$$.
This is f′ at the matching input; the inverse's derivative is its reciprocal.
Correct. Solve $$f(x) = 10$$ to get $$x \approx 1.847$$, then $$g'(10) = \frac{1}{f'(1.847)}$$.

questions.explanation: Use the calculator to solve $$f(x) = 10$$: $$x \approx 1.847$$, so $$g(10) \approx 1.847$$. Then $$g'(10) = \frac{1}{f'(g(10))} \approx \frac{1}{11.852} \approx 0.084$$.
